title: Whining noise when accelerating
h1: Why does my car whine when I accelerate?
metaDesc: Car whines when you accelerate? Answer a few questions to tell the transmission, differential, alternator or power steering apart, and how urgent it is.
synonyms: whining sound when I press the gas
whining noise that gets louder as I speed up
car makes a whining noise when driving
whining noise from engine when revving
intro: A whine that rises as you accelerate usually comes from something spinning fast: a belt-driven part on the engine, the transmission, or the differential. A simple test in Park helps separate engine-driven parts from the drivetrain. Answer the questions below to narrow down likely causes and how urgent it is.
safety: If the temperature gauge goes into the red or you see steam, pull over and shut the engine off.
If the engine revs but the car doesn't speed up, or it slips out of gear, stop driving as soon as it's safe.
If the steering suddenly gets very heavy, slow down and pull over carefully.

q_danger.q: Along with the whine, do you notice any of these?

opts.a: The engine revs up but the car doesn't speed up, or it slips or bangs into gear
The temperature gauge is climbing, or the steering suddenly feels heavy
The battery light is on, or the lights dim and flicker
None of these, just the whine

q_park_test.q: With the car in Park (or Neutral with the parking brake on), gently rev the engine. Do you hear the same whine?
q_park_test.help: Parts driven by the engine's belt, like the alternator and power steering pump, whine whenever the engine revs. The transmission, axles and differential usually only whine when the car is moving.

opts.a: Yes, it whines when I rev in Park
No, it only whines while driving
It gets louder when I turn the steering wheel
It sounds electrical, or the headlights pulse along with it
A whistle or siren that rises sharply when I accelerate hard (turbocharged engine)
A steady whine or squeal from the front of the engine, near the belts

q_driving_whine.q: While driving, which best describes the whine?

opts.a: It changes pitch when the transmission shifts, or it's tied to engine speed in each gear
It rises with road speed and changes when I let off the gas (rear-wheel, 4WD or AWD vehicle)
It's an electric or hybrid car, and it's a smooth, faint whine that's always been there

result.title: The transmission may be slipping. Driving on can cause major damage
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and check under the car for red or pink fluid. Have it towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual) rather than driving further.
if: If you find the transmission fluid is low on a car with a dipstick, adding the correct fluid may help, but have it checked before relying on it.
If the car won't move at all, turn on your hazard lights and call roadside assistance.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: A whine together with revs that climb without the car speeding up often means the transmission isn't gripping properly. Low fluid is a common reason. Continuing to drive can overheat and destroy the transmission, and it can lose drive without warning.

causes.name: Low transmission fluid from a leak
causes.clues: Red or pink drips under the middle of the car, or a burnt smell.

causes.name: Worn clutches or bands inside the transmission
causes.clues: Slipping that has been getting worse over weeks, especially in one gear.

causes.name: Torque converter or CVT problem
causes.clues: A whine and shudder when pulling away, or a loud whine that rises with engine speed.

you: Look for red or pink fluid under the car.
Check the transmission fluid level if your car has a dipstick for it, following the owner's manual.
shop: Transmission fluid level and condition check

result.title: A belt or belt-driven pump may be failing
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe and shut the engine off. Once it cools, check whether the belt is still in place, then have the car towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual) rather than driving on.
if: If the temperature gauge went into the red, don't restart the engine. Overheating can seriously damage it.
If you see coolant leaking from the front of the engine, the water pump may have failed.
If the steering went heavy, expect it to take much more effort until the car is stopped. Slow down gradually and steer gently.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: On many engines one belt drives the water pump, power steering pump and alternator. A whining bearing that seizes, or a belt that slips or breaks, can make the engine overheat and the steering go heavy within minutes.

causes.name: Failing water pump bearing
causes.clues: A whine from the front of the engine, coolant drips near the pump, and a rising temperature gauge.

causes.name: Slipping or broken drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal before the problem started, then heavy steering and a battery light.

causes.name: Seized idler or tensioner pulley
causes.clues: A loud whine or squeal that got worse quickly, then the belt came off.

you: With the engine off and cool, check that the belt is on its pulleys and not frayed.
Look for coolant drips at the front of the engine.

result.title: The alternator or charging system may be the source
result.now: Have the battery and charging system tested within a few days. Many auto parts stores can run this test. Avoid long trips and night driving until then.
if: If the battery light comes on and stays on, avoid driving any distance. The car may stall once the battery runs down, and steering and braking can then take much more effort. Have it checked as soon as you can, or towed if you're not close.
If you smell burning or the engine bay smells hot, pull over and shut the engine off.
If the temperature gauge rises or the steering suddenly gets heavy, the drive belt may have come off. Pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: The alternator spins fast and makes electricity as you drive. A worn bearing whines, and a failing internal part can make an electrical whine that rises with engine speed. If it stops charging, the car runs on the battery until it goes flat.

causes.name: Worn alternator bearing
causes.clues: A whine from the alternator that rises with engine speed, even in Park.

causes.name: Failing alternator diode or regulator
causes.clues: A whine through the radio speakers, dimming lights, or a battery light.

causes.name: Worn idler or tensioner pulley
causes.clues: The whine is from the belt area but not directly at the alternator. A shop will usually listen with a stethoscope or spin the pulleys by hand before replacing the alternator.

you: Watch for the battery light while driving.
Note whether the lights pulse or dim with engine speed.
shop: Charging system and alternator output test

result.title: Low power steering fluid or a worn pump may be the cause
result.now: With the engine off, check the power steering fluid level against the marks on the reservoir, and top it up with the fluid type in your owner's manual if it's low.
if: If the fluid was low, look for a leak and have it checked within a few days. Fluid doesn't get used up on its own.
If the whine stays after topping up, book a check. If the steering feels heavy or jerky, have it checked before driving further.
If your car has electric power steering with no fluid reservoir, a whine needs a shop to check it.
If fluid is dripping near the exhaust, or you smell burning, pull over and turn the engine off. Power steering fluid can catch fire on hot parts.
result.why: A hydraulic power steering pump works hardest when you turn the wheel, so a whine that rises when steering often points to it. Low fluid makes the pump suck in air and whine, and a worn pump whines even when full.

causes.name: Low power steering fluid
causes.clues: The reservoir is below the mark, or there's oily residue on hoses or under the front of the car.

causes.name: Worn power steering pump
causes.clues: The fluid is full, but the whine is loudest at full lock.

causes.name: Air or old fluid in the system
causes.clues: The fluid looks foamy or dark.

you: Check the power steering fluid level and color.
Look for leaks around the pump, hoses and steering rack.

result.title: Some turbo whistle is normal, but a louder siren needs a check
result.now: Book a check when convenient if the sound is new or louder than it used to be. Make sure the oil is full and changed on schedule, since turbos depend on clean oil.
if: If you see blue or gray smoke from the exhaust, or the oil level drops, get it checked within a few days.
If the engine loses power or a warning light comes on, get it checked soon.
If there's a grinding or scraping sound from the turbo, stop driving and have it towed.
If you see heavy smoke or the oil warning light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Turbochargers spin very fast and naturally make a light whistle when they build boost. A loud siren-like whine that's new can mean worn turbo bearings or a boost leak from a loose or split hose.

causes.name: Normal turbo spool sound
causes.clues: A light whistle you've always heard when accelerating.
causes.against: If it's new or much louder, something else is more likely.

causes.name: Boost leak from a loose clamp or split hose
causes.clues: A whoosh or whistle with less power than usual.

causes.name: Worn turbocharger bearings
causes.clues: A loud siren whine, oil use, or blue smoke.

you: Look for loose or split hoses between the turbo and the engine.

result.title: Often a worn wheel the belt runs on, or another belt-driven part (pulley bearing)
result.now: Book a check within the next week or two. With the engine off, look at the belt for cracks or glazing.
if: If the noise gets much louder, turns into a grind, or the battery light comes on, get it checked within a few days.
If the belt breaks, the engine can overheat and the steering can go heavy. Pull over right away if that happens.
If you smell burning rubber or see smoke from the engine bay, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: The front of the engine has several pulleys turned by one or more belts. When a pulley bearing wears, it whines in step with engine speed, in Park or driving. Catching it early can prevent a broken belt. A shop will usually check each pulley with the belt off before deciding which part to replace.

causes.name: Worn idler or tensioner pulley
causes.clues: A steady whine or rumble from the belt area that changes with engine speed.

causes.name: Worn alternator bearing
causes.clues: The whine is loudest at the alternator.

causes.name: Worn water pump bearing
causes.clues: Coolant seepage near the pump.

you: With the engine off, look at the belt for cracks or a shiny, glazed surface.
Record a short video with sound with the hood open.

result.title: The transmission may be the source of the whine
result.now: Have the transmission fluid level and condition checked within a few days. Avoid towing or heavy loads until then.
if: If the transmission starts slipping, shifting harshly or a warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If you see red or pink fluid under the car, mention it. A leak can quickly lead to low fluid.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: A whine that changes when the transmission shifts is likely coming from inside it. Low or worn-out fluid is a common cause and is much cheaper to fix early. Worn bearings, a torque converter or a CVT belt can also whine.

causes.name: Low or old transmission fluid
causes.clues: A leak, a burnt smell, or no fluid service on a high-mileage car.

causes.name: Worn torque converter or pump
causes.clues: A whine that's loudest when pulling away and changes with engine speed.

causes.name: CVT wear
causes.clues: On a car with a CVT (no distinct gear shifts), a whine or drone that's getting louder.

you: Look for red or pink fluid under the car.
Check the transmission fluid if your car has a dipstick, following the owner's manual.
shop: Transmission fluid level and condition check

result.title: The gears that drive the wheels may be the source, from low oil or wear (differential)
result.now: Have the differential fluid checked within a few days, and avoid towing or heavy loads until then.
if: If the whine becomes a grind or clunk, or you see gear oil leaking near the axle, stop driving and have it towed.
If the fluid is low, topping it up may quiet it. A shop will usually check the fluid for metal before deciding whether parts are worn.
If you feel a new vibration, or smell hot gear oil or burning near the rear axle, pull over and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: The differential sends power to the drive wheels through a set of gears in thick gear oil. Worn gears or bearings, or low oil, make a whine that rises with road speed and changes when you switch between accelerating and coasting.

causes.name: Low or worn-out differential fluid
causes.clues: Oily residue on the differential, or the fluid has never been changed.

causes.name: Worn ring and pinion gears
causes.clues: A whine mostly when accelerating at certain speeds.

causes.name: Worn pinion or carrier bearings
causes.clues: A whine or growl that's worse when coasting or decelerating.

you: Look for oil leaking from the differential housing.
Note whether the whine is worse when accelerating or coasting.
shop: Differential fluid level and condition check
Road test and chassis microphone test

result.title: A faint whine is often normal in electric and hybrid cars
result.now: Notice whether the sound is the same as it has always been. A smooth, faint whine that rises with speed is typical of the electric motor and its gears.
if: If the whine gets louder, changes in tone, or comes with a warning light or vibration, book a check with a shop that works on hybrids or EVs.
If you hear grinding or clunking, get it checked within a few days.
If a red warning light comes on, power drops suddenly, or you smell burning, pull over when it's safe, turn the car off and contact a shop or roadside assistance before driving further.
result.why: Electric motors and their reduction gears spin very fast and make a light whine, which you notice more because there's no engine noise to cover it. Some cars also play an artificial sound at low speed so pedestrians can hear them.

causes.name: Normal electric motor and gear noise
causes.clues: A smooth whine that has always been there and rises with speed.
causes.against: If it's new or getting louder, wear is more likely.

causes.name: Pedestrian warning sound
causes.clues: A hum or whine heard mostly at low speeds, from the front of the car.

causes.name: Worn reduction gear or bearing
causes.clues: The whine is louder than before, or there's a vibration.

you: Compare the sound with a similar car, or record it now so you can tell if it changes later.
shop: Road test by a hybrid or EV technician

result.title: A driveline whine needs a road test to pin down
result.now: Book a road test and inspection within the next week or two. Tell the shop the whine only happens while driving, not when revving in Park.
if: If the transmission starts slipping or shifting oddly, get it checked within a few days.
If you hear grinding or feel a new vibration, get it checked soon.
If you smell burning, see smoke, a warning light comes on or the car loses drive, pull over and have it towed.
result.why: A whine that only happens while moving comes from something that turns with the wheels or carries power to them: the transmission, the differential, or a wheel bearing. A technician can usually tell them apart on a road test.

causes.name: Transmission noise
causes.clues: The whine changes with gear shifts.

causes.name: Differential noise
causes.clues: The whine rises with road speed and changes between accelerating and coasting.

causes.name: Worn wheel bearing
causes.clues: More of a hum or growl that changes when you steer left or right.

you: Look for fluid leaks under the car.
Note the speed and gear when the whine is loudest.
